content: Lactic acidosis and severe hepatomegaly with steatosis, including fatal cases, have been reported in patients treated with nucleoside analogues, either alone or in combination with other antiretrovirals, such as lamivudine. Patients with known risk factors for liver disease should be treated with EPIVIR cautiously, although cases have also been observed in individuals without any identifiable risk factors. If a patient develops clinical or laboratory findings indicative of lactic acidosis or significant hepatotoxicity, such as hepatomegaly or steatosis (even in the absence of elevated transaminase levels), treatment with EPIVIR should be discontinued immediately. In patients co-infected with HIV-1 and hepatitis B virus (HBV), discontinuation of lamivudine has been associated with exacerbations of hepatitis. Clinical trials in non-HIV-1-infected patients with chronic hepatitis B have shown that stopping lamivudine treatment can lead to hepatitis flares, often identified by elevated serum ALT levels and the reappearance of HBV DNA. While most of these events are self-limiting, fatalities have been reported. Similar exacerbations have been observed in HIV-1/HBV co-infected patients after switching from lamivudine-containing regimens to those without lamivudine. The exact relationship between lamivudine discontinuation and these events remains unclear. Patients should be closely monitored clinically and through laboratory tests for several months after stopping lamivudine. There is insufficient evidence to determine whether restarting lamivudine alters the course of these post-treatment hepatitis exacerbations. EPIVIR contains a higher dose of lamivudine than EPIVIR-HBV, which is specifically formulated for chronic hepatitis B. The dosage and formulation of EPIVIR-HBV are not suitable for patients co-infected with HIV-1 and HBV. Using EPIVIR-HBV in such patients can lead to rapid development of HIV-1 resistance due to subtherapeutic dosing and inappropriate monotherapy. For co-infected patients, lamivudine should be administered as part of a combination antiretroviral regimen using products such as EPIVIR, COMBIVIR, EPZICOM, or TRIZIVIR. In patients treated with lamivudine for chronic hepatitis B, the emergence of lamivudine-resistant HBV variants has been observed, which is associated with reduced treatment efficacy. Similarly, lamivudine-resistant HBV variants have been reported in HIV-1-infected patients receiving lamivudine-containing antiretroviral regimens. EPIVIR should not be used concurrently with other lamivudine-containing products, such as EPIVIR-HBV, COMBIVIR, EPZICOM, or TRIZIVIR, or with emtricitabine-containing products, including ATRIPLA, EMTRIVA, TRUVADA, or COMPLERA. Ribavirin has been shown in vitro to reduce the phosphorylation of pyrimidine nucleoside analogues like lamivudine. Although no pharmacokinetic or pharmacodynamic interactions have been observed in HIV-1/HCV co-infected patients receiving ribavirin and lamivudine, hepatic decompensation, including fatal cases, has occurred in patients receiving combination antiretroviral therapy for HIV-1 along with interferon alfa, with or without ribavirin. Patients receiving EPIVIR alongside interferon alfa, with or without ribavirin, should be closely monitored for treatment-related toxicities, particularly hepatic decompensation. If clinical toxicities worsen, such as hepatic decompensation (e.g., Child-Pugh score >6), discontinuation of EPIVIR, dose reduction, or discontinuation of interferon alfa and/or ribavirin should be considered. If clinical signs, symptoms, or laboratory abnormalities suggestive of pancreatitis occur, EPIVIR treatment should be stopped immediately. Immune reconstitution syndrome has been reported in patients receiving combination antiretroviral therapy, including EPIVIR. During the initial phase of treatment, patients with immune recovery may develop inflammatory responses to latent or residual opportunistic infections, such as Mycobacterium avium, cytomegalovirus, Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, or tuberculosis. These conditions may require further evaluation and treatment. Autoimmune disorders, such as Graves’ disease, polymyositis, and Guillain-Barré syndrome, have also been reported in the context of immune reconstitution. These autoimmune conditions may have a delayed onset, occurring months after the initiation of treatment. Redistribution or accumulation of body fat has been observed in patients receiving antiretroviral therapy. This may manifest as central obesity, dorsocervical fat enlargement (buffalo hump), peripheral wasting, facial wasting, breast enlargement, or a Cushingoid appearance. The mechanism and long-term consequences of these changes are not yet fully understood, and a direct causal relationship has not been established.
